A teacher can close off a line of inquiry before hearing the reasoning that prompted it. In an episode discussed by Cowie and colleagues, a teacher dismissed an unexpected answer without first exploring the students' reasoning about how animals could be compared (Cowie et al., 2018). The exchange illustrates a difficulty that arises when teachers interpret students' developing ideas and decide which contributions warrant further attention (Krist et al., 2023). Students' epistemic agency is implicated in these judgments. Their opportunities to participate in scientific knowledge-making depend partly on whether their ideas can influence the questions being pursued and the work undertaken to investigate them (Miller et al., 2018; Stroupe, 2014).

-

Such decisions occur within lessons whose purposes and resources have often been established in advance. Teachers can create opportunities for students to contribute to the direction of inquiry, but sustaining that inquiry requires attention to disciplinary goals and the support students need to develop explanations (Ko & Krist, 2019; DeCoito, 2024). A Grade 6 investigation of flight illustrates how these responsibilities can come into tension. As students worked with materials, their investigations challenged the sequence of knowledge-building activities the teacher had prepared (Reeve, 2023). The difficulty extends beyond accommodating an unexpected question. Teachers must decide how the question might be investigated, what scientific relationships require attention, and how the available time and materials can support that work.

Students may also have considerable freedom to select an inquiry topic while exercising less influence over the decisions that follow. In a Grade 7 Science and Technology project, students chose to investigate Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and prepared a public Red Dress exhibition. Some nevertheless reported that peers overlooked their contributions during collaboration (Jao et al., 2026). Another dimension of participation emerges when students help determine how an investigation should proceed. During a seventh-grade biology unit on stress, students questioned whether a proposed community survey might upset respondents. Their concerns became part of discussions with adults about responsible evidence gathering (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2026). These accounts locate student influence at different points in inquiry, from choosing a direction to negotiating the practices and criteria through which the work is carried out.

-

The distinction raises questions about who is authorized to judge scientific work. Productive disciplinary engagement connects students' authority with their responsibilities toward a shared problem and the resources available for investigating it (Engle & Conant, 2002). Rightful presence brings attention to the historically unequal conditions through which particular contributions and challenges to established practices become recognizable and legitimate (Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2020). A classroom may invite students to develop explanations while leaving the standards for evaluating those explanations entirely with the teacher. Therefore, examining participation requires attention to what students can contribute and to the opportunities they have to question the grounds on which their contributions are judged.

-

Teachers' professional conversations offer another setting in which these judgments can be examined. Sustained professional learning has supported science teachers in attending more closely to students' epistemic practices, and collaborative instructional-material development creates opportunities to reconsider classroom approaches (Shim & Thompson, 2022; Jao & McDougall, 2015). However, the focus of collaboration can shape which aspects of student thinking receive scrutiny. In rehearsals of mathematical defining, participants discussed pedagogical approaches more extensively than students' reasoning about definitions (Kobiela et al., 2023). Although the disciplinary context differs, the finding raises a relevant question for science teacher learning. When teachers examine a lesson together, how often do they investigate the reasoning behind students' contributions, including contributions that seem inconsistent with the lesson's anticipated direction?
